title: 1 Samuel 14:36–46
context: 1 Samuel 14:36–46 brings the crisis of Saul’s oath to a head. Saul wants to pursue the Philistines through the night, but at the priest’s urging he asks God first, and God does not answer. Concluding that some sin is to blame, Saul swears that the guilty one will die even if it is his son Jonathan. By lot, first Saul and Jonathan are taken, then Jonathan alone. Jonathan admits tasting the honey, and Saul pronounces his death. The people intervene: Jonathan has “worked this great salvation in Israel” and “worked with God today,” so they rescue him. The narrative presents the people’s judgment favorably, and Saul abandons the pursuit.

verses.text: Saul said, “Let’s go down after the Philistines by night, and take plunder among them until the morning light. Let’s not leave a man of them.” They said, “Do whatever seems good to you.” Then the priest said, “Let’s draw near here to God.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul proposes a night pursuit, the people agree, and the priest says, “Let’s draw near here to God.” Arminian readers note that the priest prompts Saul to seek God before acting, a right step that Saul had cut short in 14:19. The people defer to Saul’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the priest, not Saul, initiates the inquiry. Saul’s plans are driven by his desire to finish the battle, and he needs reminding to consult God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the value of seeking God before acting, and both note that Saul’s instinct is again to press ahead.

verses.text: Saul asked counsel of God: “Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you deliver them into the hand of Israel?” But he didn’t answer him that day.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul asks, “Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you deliver them into the hand of Israel?” But God does not answer him that day. Arminian readers note that God’s silence is meaningful. Something has disrupted Israel’s relationship with God, prompting Saul to look for the cause.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s silence is itself a response, signaling that all is not well. Later, God’s refusal to answer Saul becomes a sign of his rejection (compare 28:6). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that God is not obliged to answer on demand and that his silence calls for self-examination.

verses.text: Saul said, “Draw near here, all you chiefs of the people, and know and see in whom this sin has been today.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul summons the leaders to “know and see in whom this sin has been today.” Arminian readers note that Saul assumes the problem lies with someone else. He does not consider that his own rash oath might be the cause of the trouble.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul’s instinct is right that God’s silence calls for investigation, but he looks for a culprit rather than examining himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the narrative’s portrait of Saul, whose zeal is real but whose self-awareness is lacking.

verses.text: For as the LORD lives, who saves Israel, though it is in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die.” But there was not a man among all the people who answered him.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul swears, “as the LORD lives, who saves Israel, though it is in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die.” No one answers him. Arminian readers note that the people’s silence suggests they know what Jonathan did and are unwilling to condemn him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony of Saul’s oath, which invokes the LORD “who saves Israel” while threatening the one through whom God has just saved Israel. A second rash oath compounds the first. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a further example of Saul’s rash speech, which the narrative will show to be mistaken.

verses.text: Then he said to all Israel, “You be on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side.” The people said to Saul, “Do what seems good to you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul divides the assembly, with himself and Jonathan on one side and the people on the other. The people say, “Do what seems good to you.” Arminian readers note that the people defer to Saul, though their earlier silence hinted at their reluctance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the arrangement places Saul and Jonathan under scrutiny together, foreshadowing the outcome. The people’s repeated deference contrasts with their decisive intervention in 14:45. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as preparation for the lot, and neither finds a doctrinal contrast in it.

verses.text: Therefore Saul said to the LORD, the God of Israel, “Show the right.” Jonathan and Saul were chosen, but the people escaped.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul prays to the LORD, “Show the right,” and Jonathan and Saul are chosen, while the people escape. Arminian readers note that the lot narrows the matter to the king and his son, confirming that the issue lies within Saul’s house. Saul’s request asks God to make the truth plain rather than leaving it to human suspicion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Proverbs 16:33 says of the lot that “its every decision is from the LORD.” The lot here identifies Jonathan’s breach of the oath. Shared ground: both traditions read the lot as revealing the facts of the case, while the narrative goes on to show that it does not settle whether Jonathan deserved death.

verses.text: Saul said, “Cast lots between me and Jonathan my son.” Jonathan was selected.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul says, “Cast lots between me and Jonathan my son,” and Jonathan is selected. Arminian readers note that Saul presses the process to its end, even though it now points toward his own son. His determination to keep his oath overrides other concerns.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the lot confirms that Jonathan broke the oath, but the narrative has already shown that he did so unknowingly (14:27). Shared ground: both traditions distinguish the fact the lot reveals from the moral judgment that follows, and both read the outcome in light of the people’s verdict in 14:45.

verses.text: Then Saul said to Jonathan, “Tell me what you have done!” Jonathan told him, and said, “I certainly did taste a little honey with the end of the rod that was in my hand; and behold, I must die.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul demands, “Tell me what you have done!” Jonathan says, “I certainly did taste a little honey … and behold, I must die.” Arminian readers note Jonathan’s honesty. He does not hide or excuse what he did, though his words may also carry a note of protest at so harsh a penalty for so little.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jonathan’s confession is truthful and submissive. Unlike Achan, whose hidden sin brought trouble, Jonathan acted openly and in ignorance. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing Jonathan’s integrity and as highlighting the disproportion between his act and the threatened penalty.

verses.text: Saul said, “God do so and more also; for you shall surely die, Jonathan.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul says, “God do so and more also; for you shall surely die, Jonathan.” Arminian readers note that Saul is ready to sacrifice his son rather than appear to break his oath. His rigidity puts the appearance of piety above justice and wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul’s insistence recalls Jephthah’s tragic vow, “I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I can’t go back” (Judges 11:35). A rash oath leads to a terrible outcome. Shared ground: both traditions read Saul’s words as the climax of his rashness, which the people will rightly refuse to carry out.

verses.text: The people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As the LORD lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground, for he has worked with God today!” So the people rescued Jonathan, so he didn’t die.
verses.arminianNotes: The people say, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! … he has worked with God today!” They rescue Jonathan. Arminian readers note that the people recognize God’s hand in Jonathan’s actions and refuse to punish him for an act done in ignorance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the people’s verdict, “he has worked with God today,” is the narrative’s own evaluation. The Hebrew verb behind “rescued” is the one often rendered “ransomed.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as vindicating Jonathan and as a rebuke to Saul’s rash oath, showing that the people discerned God’s work more clearly than their king.

verses.text: Then Saul went up from following the Philistines; and the Philistines went to their own place.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul stops pursuing the Philistines, and they return to their own place. Arminian readers note the limited result: the victory God gave was cut short by the disruption of Saul’s oath. The Philistine threat remains.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the episode ends without the complete victory Jonathan had hoped for (14:30). Saul’s rashness has cost Israel. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober ending, showing that God’s deliverance was real but that human folly limited its scope.
